newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court okays probe into official wiretaps.
newsitem.headline: French court okays probe into official wiretaps.

text.p: A French appeals court on Monday authorised a magistrate to pursue a probe into illegal wiretaps of journalists and politicians by a presidential anti-terrorist unit under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

Paris' state prosecutor had ordered investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Valat to drop the case on the grounds that the bugging of some 150 people between 1983 and 1986 was covered by a three-year statute of limitations.
But the appeals court ruled that invasion of privacy was covered by the statute of limitations from the moment it became known to the victims and not from the time it took place.

Sitting at the request of some of those who were bugged, the court also ruled that the statute of limitations in the case was 10 years since the wiretaps infringed on individual rights guaranteed by the constitution.
The presidential palace's anti-terrorist squad has since been disbanded.
The wiretaps were revealed by the centre-left newspaper Liberation three years ago, but the list of wiretap targets, possibly still incomplete, only came out later.
Six former Mitterrand administration officials, including his ex-cabinet chief, Gilles Menage, have been placed under investigation and could face jail terms if convicted.
One of them, paramilitary gendarmerie officer Pierre-Yves Guezou, has killed himself.
Under the law, wiretaps are legal when dealing with national security, terrorist threats or protecting essential scientific or economic information, but must be authorised by a judge.
None of the taps involved was authorised or dealt with national security or terrorism.

Many focused on personal matters including one directed at a writer preparing a book about Mitterrand's private life which would have disclosed that he lived with his mistress and their daughter, both of whom were then unknown to the public.
Another wiretap was directed at a famous actress said to be amorously pursued by a senior presidential aide jealous of her other admirers.

Critics have said the current centre-right government was not eager to have the case go to trial, even though the events took place under Mitterrand's presidency, because it could expose possible illegal taps under the new administration.
An official panel said earlier this year that about 100,000 telephone lines are illegally tapped each year in the country and state agencies may be behind much of the eavesdropping.

Curbs imposed on wiretapping by official bodies may have just tempted them to farm out their illegal bugging out to private firms, the independent National Commission for the Control of Security Interceptions said in its annual report.
